name: horn

attributes.attribute: mark of the god of male power in Celtic art
the horned one, with a stag's antlers, represented plenty
reworked in Christian times a sign of the Devil
may stand for leadership and power

text: The horn is a symbolic object. Horns and antlers number among the chief marks of the Celtic god of male vigor. Ancient images place them on many deities. Two main forms of the horned God exist. The first form has the antlers of a stag and sits cross-legged, staring forward. A writing on a Paris statue matched this god to Cernunnos, the horned one. Cernunnos stood for plenty. The image sometimes has three heads. The Gaulish gods Mercury and Cocidius sometimes took horns, showing the way to the horned god. The second form of horn sets the horns of cattle or other stock on the heads of male gods. Such images give no mark beyond the horns for the god's nature. Since warriors and leaders wore horned helmets, the horns may stand for leadership and power. Goddesses also wore horns, but far less often. A goddess wore antlers, like a female deer, or sometimes the horn of the bull or goat. Such a goddess showed the animal power of the earth and the bond between a woman and the wild. A wonder truly Celtic was the ram-headed snake. Christian times made its image into a sign of evil. The Devil with ram's horns descends straight from this older god-image. Some folk rites still held, as at Abbots Bromley, the old horned god.

okr.objective: Document the horn as a symbol of the horned god and goddess in Celtic tradition
key_results: the two forms of the horned god, antlered and bull-horned.
